title: The jobs of HTML, CSS and JavaScript

choices.a: Wrong. This swaps HTML and CSS. HTML gives the text and structure, such as headings and lists, and CSS gives the colors and fonts.
choices.b: Correct. HTML gives the content and structure, CSS gives the look, and JavaScript adds behavior, such as what happens on a click. These are the basic roles, not strict rules: HTML alone can show extra details on a click, with the `<details>` and `<summary>` elements. But the language that is mainly responsible for click behavior is JavaScript, and no other choice matches the first two parts.
choices.c: Wrong. This swaps CSS and JavaScript. CSS sets the colors and fonts, and JavaScript controls what happens when you click a button.
choices.d: Wrong. HTML, not JavaScript, gives the headings, paragraphs and lists. JavaScript, not HTML, is mainly responsible for what happens on a click.

tutorial:
A browser shows a web page from code in three languages. Each language has a main job: | Language | Main job | Examples | |---|---|---| | **HTML** (HyperText Markup Language) | Content and structure | Headings, paragraphs, bullet lists, tables, links, buttons | | **CSS** (Cascading Style Sheets) | Look and feel | Colors, fonts, spacing, layout | | **JavaScript** (JS) | Interactivity (behavior) | What happens when you click or hover; changing the page without reloading it | HTML is written with **tags**, such as `

` and `

`. CSS is written as **rules** that say how things look. JavaScript looks like a usual programming language, with functions, `if`/`else` and loops. You can keep each language in its own file (`.html`, `.css`, `.js`), or you can put all three in one `.html` file. These jobs are the basic idea, not strict rules. HTML can control some of the look, and JavaScript can create text and change the HTML and CSS. HTML also has a few elements with built-in behavior: for example, `
` and `` show or hide extra text on a click. When a question asks which language is *mainly* responsible, use the main jobs in the table.
